content: The inpatient treatment of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in infants under six months of age is a critical area of global health that has historically been under-researched and under-prioritized. SAM is a significant public health issue, contributing to over one million child deaths annually. While most efforts have focused on children aged six months to five years, there is growing recognition that infants under six months are also at risk and require specific attention. This review, commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO), aims to address the evidence gap in the treatment of SAM in this vulnerable age group. Background Severe acute malnutrition in infants under six months of age (referred to as infants <6m) has often been overlooked due to misconceptions that exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) protects this group from malnutrition. However, global rates of EBF are alarmingly low, with only 25–31% of infants aged 2–5 months being exclusively breastfed. Additionally, the adoption of the WHO Child Growth Standards has revealed a higher prevalence of SAM in this age group than previously recognized. Despite these findings, treatment strategies for infants <6m remain challenging due to their unique nutritional needs and the emphasis on re-establishing EBF, which requires skilled staff and significant time investment. Methods This review involved two main components: 1. Analysis of National Guidelines: The Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation (AGREE) framework was used to assess 36 national SAM guidelines, focusing on their recommendations for treating infants <6m. 2. Literature Review: A systematic review of published studies was conducted using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach to evaluate evidence on therapeutic feeding strategies, feeding protocols, and treatment outcomes for infants <6m. Key Findings National Guidelines Of the 36 national guidelines reviewed, 29 (81%) included specific sections on SAM in infants <6m. However, the space devoted to this age group was limited, averaging only 6% of the total guideline content. All 29 guidelines recommended inpatient care for infants <6m with SAM, but only one distinguished between complicated and uncomplicated cases, as is done for older children. Supplementary suckling (SS) was the core treatment method recommended in 28 of the 29 guidelines, aiming to re-establish effective EBF. Strengths of the guidelines included clear scope and purpose, professional stakeholder involvement, and good presentation. Weaknesses included a lack of patient involvement, poor methodological rigor, and limited editorial independence. Therapeutic Feeding Strategies Evidence on the safest and most effective therapeutic feeding strategies during the stabilization, transition, and rehabilitation phases of treatment was limited. For stabilization feeds, infant formula at 100 kcal/kg/day was identified as a strong option due to its similarity to breast milk and low renal solute load. However, this recommendation was conditional on the availability of appropriate feeds. For transition and rehabilitation phases, breast milk substitutes (BMS) such as F-100 or formula were recommended for non-breastfed infants, while breastfed infants were encouraged to transition back to EBF. Feeding Protocols Feeding protocols emphasized gradually increasing feed volumes for non-breastfed infants and re-establishing breastfeeding wherever possible. Most guidelines recommended feeding every three hours for at least 20 minutes, with additional feeds if the infant was willing. For infants with the potential to breastfeed, supplementary suckling was the preferred method to stimulate breast milk production while providing additional nutrition. Systemic Treatments Vitamin A supplementation was recommended in 86% of guidelines, with most suggesting a dose of 50,000 IU upon admission. First-line antibiotics were recommended in 86% of guidelines, with amoxicillin being the most commonly prescribed. However, dosing regimens varied widely. Iron supplementation was recommended in 79% of guidelines but was generally delayed until the infant showed signs of improvement. Challenges and Opportunities The lack of high-quality evidence for treating SAM in infants <6m presents both a challenge and an opportunity. Current guidelines are based on low-quality evidence, highlighting the need for further research to improve treatment protocols. Despite limited evidence, many countries have made significant advances in addressing SAM in infants <6m within their protocols. However, these approaches often differ from those used for older children, with no separation of complicated and uncomplicated cases and no outpatient-based care models. Recommendations Infants <6m should be divided into two groups: those with and without the potential to breastfeed. This distinction is critical for tailoring treatment strategies. Low-birth-weight (LBW) infants should follow the WHO 2010 LBW guidelines, which may also apply to SAM infants of unknown birth weight. Future research should focus on developing evidence-based guidelines for outpatient care and public health-focused models for managing SAM in infants <6m. Conclusion Addressing SAM in infants <6m is a pressing global health priority. While current evidence is limited, acknowledging the problem and implementing targeted interventions can significantly improve outcomes for this vulnerable population. With early-life nutrition now high on the political agenda, there is a unique opportunity to advance research and improve care for infants <6m with SAM.
